items: Count how many audit questions you answered 'no' to and note that answering 'no' to 3 or more means you received a template instead of personalized advice.

Check whether your consultant asked about medical history, feeding schedules, and developmental changes before giving any sleep advice because genuine customization requires understanding your child's full context.
Verify that your consultant explained why their method works specifically for toddlers rather than just citing generic infant sleep principles that don't apply to children over 18 months.
Confirm that your consultant provided a clear protocol for what to do if your child's sleep worsened, not just instructions for the ideal scenario where everything goes smoothly.
Accept that by 18 months your toddler understands object permanence and knows you are choosing to leave them alone, which makes cry-it-out fundamentally different than with infants.
Recognize that separation anxiety peaking around 18 months is a developmental stage rooted in attachment awareness that should not be treated as a behavior to be trained away.
Understand that toddlers form emotional memories and may develop a conditioned fear response to the bedroom or crib after prolonged crying episodes during sleep training.
Stop comparing toddler sleep methods to infant methods because the developmental contexts are entirely different and what works for a 6-month-old may harm a 22-month-old.
Extend wake windows to 4-6 hours of awake time before your toddler's longest sleep period since the 2-3 hour windows used for infants no longer apply after 18 months.
Try a later bedtime if your toddler is in an overtiredness spiral since an earlier bedtime can cause a cortisol spike that makes falling asleep harder, not easier.
Fill your child's emotional tank by spending device-free time together in the hour before bed as a daily practice, not a reward for going to sleep, to reduce overnight escalation.
Rule out medical issues and underlying conditions before starting any sleep intervention since pain, reflux, or developmental concerns can mimic or worsen sleep problems.
